title: Injectivity of the critical map and its cokernel
statement:
With $f:X\to S$ and $n$ as in [sbc-def-base-change-property], assume for
some $q\geq1$ that $\mathrm{BC}(f,n,q-1)$ holds universally (in the
single degree $q-1$; no hypothesis in the degrees $<q-1$ is needed).
Let $S'\to S$ be a morphism, $f':X'=X\times_SS'\to S'$ the base change,
$g:T\to S'$ a quasi-compact and quasi-separated morphism, and
$h:Y=X'\times_{S'}T\to X'$, $e:Y\to T$ the projections. Then for
every abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ on $T_{\Et}$ annihilated by $n$:

1. the base-change map
$f'^{-1}R^qg_*\mathcal F\to R^qh_*e^{-1}\mathcal F$ is
injective;
1. if $\mathcal F\subset\mathcal G$ with $\mathcal G$ an abelian sheaf
on $T_{\Et}$ annihilated by $n$, then
$$
\operatorname{Coker}\bigl(f'^{-1}R^qg_*\mathcal F\to
R^qh_*e^{-1}\mathcal F\bigr)
\subset\operatorname{Coker}\bigl(f'^{-1}R^qg_*\mathcal G\to
R^qh_*e^{-1}\mathcal G\bigr);
$$
1. if in (2) the sheaf $\mathcal G$ is an injective sheaf of
$\mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z$-modules, then
$$
\operatorname{Coker}\bigl(f'^{-1}R^qg_*\mathcal F\to
R^qh_*e^{-1}\mathcal F\bigr)
\subset R^qh_*e^{-1}\mathcal G.
$$

(*Stacks Project, [Tag `0F03`](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F03).*)

proof.text: Put $A^i(E)=f\prime^{-1}R^ig_*E$ and $B^i(E)=R^ih_*e^{-1}E$, and denote the base-change arrow by $a_E^i$. Work first with $\Lambda=\mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z$-module sheaves. Enough injectives gives $0\to F\to I\to Q\to0$ with $I$ injective; $Q$ is again annihilated by $n$. Direct image is left exact, so injective acyclicity gives $R^qg_*I=0$ for $q>0$ in module sheaves. The exchange-forget-coefficients comparison identifies this with vanishing for the underlying abelian sheaf (an injective module sheaf need not itself be an injective abelian sheaf). Exactness of inverse image gives exact rows after applying the two derived functors. Their long exact sequences and base-change maps agree with those for abelian sheaves by the same coefficient comparison.

The long-exact comparison gives exact rows $A^{q-1}(I)\to A^{q-1}(Q)\to A^q(F)\to0$ and $B^{q-1}(I)\to B^{q-1}(Q)\to B^q(F)\to B^q(I)$. The first two vertical maps are isomorphisms: universal $BC(f,n,q-1)$ applies to $f\prime$, the given qcqs $g$, and the $n$-annihilated sheaves $I,Q$. Thus they induce an isomorphism of the cokernels of the first horizontal arrows. The upper cokernel is $A^q(F)$; the lower cokernel is the kernel of $B^q(F)\to B^q(I)$. Commutativity identifies this induced map with $a_F^q$. Consequently $a_F^q$ is injective and its image is exactly that kernel. This proves (1) and gives an induced monomorphism $c_{F,I}:\operatorname{Coker}(a_F^q)\to B^q(I)$.

For clause (3), run steps 1 and 2 with the specified injective sheaf $G$ in place of $I$ and the given inclusion $F\to G$; the resulting $c_{F,G}$ is the required map. For clause (2), embed $G$ into an injective $I$ using enough injectives and compose $F\to G\to I$. Apply step 2 to both $F\to I$ and $G\to I$. Naturality yields the cokernel map $d:\operatorname{Coker}(a_F^q)\to\operatorname{Coker}(a_G^q)$. By construction each $c_{E,I}$ is induced by $B^q(E)\to B^q(I)$, so functoriality of $B^q$ and the quotient universal property give $c_{G,I}\circ d=c_{F,I}$. Since $c_{F,I}$ is a monomorphism, $d$ is a monomorphism: if $d u=d v$, composing with $c_{G,I}$ and cancelling $c_{F,I}$ gives $u=v$. This proves (2).
